title: Code Quality Gates
subtitle: ESLint, Prettier, TypeScript strict checks, and SonarCloud integration — automated code quality in every PR

content.text: Why code quality belongs in CI

Code reviews are expensive human time. Code quality tools catch whole categories of issues before a human even opens the PR — unused variables, inconsistent formatting, type errors, and known anti-patterns. In CI, these tools become gates: the PR simply cannot merge until the code passes. They also make reviews more productive: reviewers focus on logic and design, not style nits.

content.code:
name: Code Quality
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  quality:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: '20', cache: 'npm' }
      - run: npm ci

      # TypeScript strict type checking
      - name: Type check
        run: npx tsc --noEmit

      # ESLint — fail on any error (warnings allowed)
      - name: Lint
        run: npx eslint . --max-warnings=0
        # --max-warnings=0: even warnings fail the job
        # Adjust to a positive number during a codebase cleanup

      # Prettier — check formatting without changing files
      - name: Format check
        run: npx prettier --check .
        # Fails if any file would be reformatted
        # Fix locally: npx prettier --write .

      # Report ESLint results as GitHub annotations (inline in PR diff)
      - name: ESLint with annotations
        if: always()
        run: |
          npx eslint . --format=@microsoft/eslint-formatter-sarif \
            --output-file eslint-results.sarif || true

      - name: Upload ESLint SARIF
        if: always()
        uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v3
        with:
          sarif_file: eslint-results.sarif
          wait-for-processing: true

# SonarCloud is free for open source projects
# Setup: sonarcloud.io → link your GitHub repo → get SONAR_TOKEN

- name: SonarCloud scan
  uses: SonarSource/sonarcloud-github-action@master
  env:
    GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
    SONAR_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.SONAR_TOKEN }}
  # SonarCloud checks:
  # - Code coverage (fails if below configured threshold)
  # - Code smells (anti-patterns, complexity)
  # - Duplicate code
  # - Security hotspots
  # - Bugs found by static analysis
  # All configurable in sonar-project.properties

sonar.projectKey=myorg_myrepo
sonar.organization=myorg

# Source files to analyse
sonar.sources=src
sonar.exclusions=**/*.test.ts,**/node_modules/**

# Coverage reports
sonar.javascript.lcov.reportPaths=coverage/lcov.info

# Quality Gate: fails the PR if coverage drops below 80%
# or if new code has any bugs/vulnerabilities
# Configure the threshold in SonarCloud project settings

content.text: Fix the root cause, not the symptom. When ESLint flags an error, understand why the rule exists. @typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises exists because unawaited promises silently swallow errors. no-console exists because console.log in production apps pollutes log infrastructure. Disabling a rule with // eslint-disable-next-line should be a last resort with a comment explaining why.

questions.question: A developer wants to skip the Prettier format check for one file. What is the correct approach?
options: Add the file to .gitignore so CI doesn't see it
Add the file path to .prettierignore — Prettier and the CI check will both skip it
Disable the format check step with 'if: false' in the workflow
Run 'prettier --write' on the file to auto-format it and commit the result
questions.explanation: The correct fix is to run 'prettier --write' locally, let Prettier reformat the file, and commit the formatted result. This keeps the file consistently formatted. .prettierignore is for files that genuinely shouldn't be formatted (generated code, binary-like text, vendor files). Adding to .gitignore would remove the file from source control entirely. Disabling the CI step defeats the purpose for everyone.

faq.q: ESLint reports thousands of errors in a legacy codebase. How do we adopt it gradually?
faq.a: Start with --max-warnings=9999 (very permissive) and commit a baseline. Then use eslint-baseline (or lint-staged for new files only) to only fail on NEW violations. Ratchet the threshold down over time. This lets you adopt quality gates without stopping all development while you fix historical issues.

examples: Google's internal codebase runs automated linters and formatters on every commit — no human reviewer ever debates semicolons or indentation; all of that is decided by the tool
SonarCloud's 'Quality Gate' can block a PR from merging if test coverage drops even 1% — teams use this to prevent gradual erosion of coverage over time
